wal: use similes and alliteration to make my descriptions more powerful
tib: Figurative language helps readers picture a place and feel its mood, making descriptions come alive on the page.
isb: writing at least three similes and three alliterative phrases that describe the city at night.

title: Grammar Warm-Up
subtitle: Which technique? Identify the figurative language in each sentence.

cards.label: Sentence A
lines: The alleyway was as cold as a grave.
Simile or alliteration?

cards.label: Sentence B
lines: Dark shadows shifted and slid silently past.
Simile or alliteration?

cards.label: Sentence C
lines: The streetlamp glowed like a tiny captured sun.
Simile or alliteration?

title: Reading like a writer
lines: S. F. Said writes the city through Varjak’s eyes.
Everything is new, strange and a little frightening.
As you listen to this passage, think:
• Can you spot any figurative language?
• What is the effect on the reader?
• How does the writer make the city feel alive?

label: Display a short passage from Varjak Paw that contains similes or alliteration

title: Simile
left_lines: A simile compares one thing to another
using the words like or as.
cars roared past like angry beasts
the street was as wide as a river
The comparison must make sense and
right_lines: For Varjak, everything in the city
is new. A simile lets us see it
through his eyes for the first time.

title: Alliteration
left_lines: sound at the start of nearby words.
The repeated sound must be at the
start of the word, not in the middle.
right_lines: draws attention to a moment or image.
It can make a sound feel louder
Use it sparingly so it has impact.

title: Build your own figurative language.
lines: Write three similes describing the city at night.
Write three alliterative phrases describing the city at night.
Think about:
• What does Varjak see, hear or smell?
• What would he compare it to?
• Which consonant sounds suit the mood?
The best examples will go straight onto the working wall.
challenge: Write one sentence that contains both a simile AND alliteration.

title: Share and add to the working wall.
lines: Listen to a few examples.
For each one, ask:
• Does the simile make you picture something more clearly?
• Does the alliteration create a sound or rhythm?
• Could we use this in our narrative?
Add the best examples to the working wall under
the right category: sights, sounds, smells or feelings.

q1: Which of your similes are you most pleased with, and why?
q2: How does alliteration change the way a sentence sounds when you read it aloud?
q3: Which technique do you think you will use most in your narrative?
